stem: A hospital grants permissions based on job roles like 'Nurse' and 'Physician,' so new hires inherit their role's access. Which access control model is MOST in use?

options.rationale: Assigning permissions to roles and granting them via role membership is RBAC, which scales well in organizations.
DAC has owners grant access at their discretion, not permissions tied to defined job roles.
MAC enforces access via labels/clearances, not job roles.
The scenario clearly uses a role-based model, not the absence of control.

stem: In a classified system, access is enforced by the operating system comparing a user's clearance to a document's classification label, and owners cannot override it. This is MOST accurately which model?

options.rationale: System-enforced access based on clearances and classification labels, not overridable by owners, is MAC.
DAC lets owners decide access, which contradicts the non-overridable label enforcement described.
RBAC uses job roles, not clearance/classification labels enforced by the system.
While ABAC uses attributes, the specific clearance-vs-label enforcement described is the defining feature of MAC.

stem: On a standard file server, the creator of a document decides which colleagues may read or edit it by setting permissions. This is MOST accurately which model?

options.rationale: The owner deciding access at their discretion (via file permissions/ACLs) is DAC — the model of standard OS file permissions.
MAC is system-enforced via labels, not owner discretion.
RBAC assigns access via roles, not individual owner discretion per file.
ABAC evaluates attribute policies, not simple owner-set file permissions.

stem: A policy states: 'Allow access if role=Physician AND device is managed AND time is within shift hours AND record belongs to the user's department.' This granular, context-aware policy MOST reflects which model?

options.rationale: Evaluating multiple attributes of subject, object, action, and environment is ABAC — the most granular, dynamic model.
DAC is owner-driven ACLs, not multi-attribute contextual policy.
MAC uses clearance/label dominance, not this multi-attribute contextual rule set.
RBAC alone uses role membership; the added device, time, and department conditions make this ABAC.

stem: A company with thousands of employees wants to simplify access administration so that changing one job function's permissions updates all its members at once. Which model BEST achieves this?

options.text: RBAC — modify the role and all members inherit the change
options.rationale: RBAC centralizes permissions in roles, so a single role change propagates to all users in that role, easing large-scale administration.

options.text: DAC — have each owner update every file individually
options.rationale: Per-file owner updates do not scale and would be enormous manual effort.

options.text: MAC — reclassify every document by hand
options.rationale: MAC label management does not map to simplifying job-function permission changes at scale.

options.text: No model — let users set their own permissions
options.rationale: Uncontrolled self-service access is insecure and unmanageable.

stem: Which access control model is characterized by the data owner deciding who may access their resources?

options.rationale: DAC is defined by owner discretion over access to their objects.
MAC is system-enforced via labels, not owner discretion.
RBAC assigns access via roles, not individual owner discretion.
This is not an access control model in this context.

stem: Which model is MOST appropriate when a strict, non-overridable, system-enforced policy is required, even at the cost of flexibility?

options.rationale: MAC provides rigid, system-enforced access that owners cannot override, ideal for the highest-security environments.
DAC is the most flexible but owner-overridable, unsuitable when a non-overridable policy is required.
RBAC organizes by roles but is not defined by non-overridable label enforcement like MAC.
Absence of control is the opposite of a strict enforced policy.

stem: A firewall permits or denies traffic based on global rules regardless of user identity. This is MOST accurately which type of access control, and how does it differ from RBAC?

options.text: Rule-based access control, which applies global rules — distinct from RBAC's role-based permissions
options.rationale: Rule-based control (like firewall ACLs) enforces global conditions, whereas RBAC grants access by user role; the exam tests this naming distinction.

options.text: It is RBAC because 'rule' and 'role' are the same
options.rationale: Rule-based and role-based are different concepts despite similar abbreviations.
The firewall applies global rules, not clearance/label dominance as in MAC.

options.text: It is DAC set by each user
options.rationale: Global firewall rules are not per-user owner discretion (DAC).

stem: Which is the MOST significant security drawback of DAC compared with MAC?

options.text: Owners can grant access at their discretion, increasing the risk of over-sharing or mistakes
options.rationale: DAC's reliance on owner discretion makes it flexible but prone to inconsistent or excessive access grants.

options.text: DAC cannot control access at all
options.rationale: DAC does control access; the drawback is discretion-based inconsistency, not lack of control.
Clearances are a MAC feature, not DAC.
Encryption is a separate control; this is not the defining DAC drawback versus MAC.

stem: Regardless of model, what is the BEST guiding principle when assigning access rights to subjects?

options.text: Grant only the minimum access needed to perform the job (least privilege)
options.rationale: Least privilege minimizes the access each subject holds, reducing risk if the account is misused or compromised, across all models.

options.text: Grant everyone administrator rights for convenience
options.rationale: Broad admin rights violate least privilege and greatly increase risk.

options.text: Give the same access to all users
options.rationale: Uniform access ignores differing needs and over-privileges many users.

options.text: Grant access based on seniority alone
options.rationale: Access should map to need/function, not seniority for its own sake.

stem: A defense agency needs access strictly governed by data classification and personnel clearance, enforced by the system. Which model is BEST?

options.rationale: MAC's clearance-and-classification enforcement is designed for exactly these high-security government/military environments.
DAC's owner discretion is too flexible for strict classified enforcement.
RBAC organizes by role but does not inherently enforce clearance/classification like MAC.
The requirement is strict enforcement, not the absence of control.

stem: Which model MOST naturally supports fine-grained, context-aware decisions such as time of day, device posture, and location?

options.rationale: ABAC evaluates rich attributes (subject, resource, action, environment), enabling the most granular, context-aware access decisions.
DAC is owner-set ACLs and does not natively evaluate contextual attributes like time/device.
MAC keys on clearance/label dominance, not arbitrary contextual attributes.
Basic RBAC keys on role membership alone, lacking the contextual attribute evaluation of ABAC.

stem: Standard file permissions on a typical operating system, where the file owner sets who can read/write, are an example of which model?

options.rationale: Owner-set file permissions are the canonical example of Discretionary Access Control.
MAC is label/clearance-enforced, not owner-set file permissions.
RBAC is role-based; standard owner-set file permissions are DAC.
ABAC uses attribute policies, not simple owner-set file permissions.

stem: An RBAC deployment creates hundreds of narrowly-defined, overlapping roles that become hard to manage. This problem is MOST accurately called what?

options.rationale: Proliferation of overly specific, overlapping roles is 'role explosion,' a known RBAC design pitfall to avoid.
Privilege escalation is gaining higher rights via a flaw, not a proliferation of roles.
This is not a standard term for the RBAC role-proliferation problem.
Clearance dominance is a MAC concept, unrelated to too many roles.

stem: Which statement MOST accurately compares DAC and MAC on the flexibility-vs-security spectrum?

options.text: DAC is more flexible but riskier; MAC is more rigid but more secure
options.rationale: DAC's owner discretion is flexible but error-prone, while MAC's system-enforced labels are rigid but provide stronger control.

options.text: MAC is more flexible than DAC
options.rationale: MAC is more rigid, not more flexible, than DAC.
DAC is overridable by owners; MAC is the non-overridable model.

options.text: Both are identical in flexibility and security
options.rationale: They differ significantly; DAC favors flexibility, MAC favors control.

stem: Under RBAC, when a new accountant is hired, what should happen FIRST to grant appropriate access?

options.text: Assign the user to the predefined 'Accountant' role
options.rationale: In RBAC, placing the user in the appropriate role grants the role's predefined permissions, the standard onboarding step.

options.text: Manually set permissions on every file individually
options.rationale: Per-file manual permissioning defeats RBAC's purpose and does not scale.

options.text: Give the user domain admin rights
options.rationale: Domain admin rights violate least privilege for an accountant role.

options.text: Grant access to all classified labels
options.rationale: Broad classified access is inappropriate and unrelated to the accountant role.

stem: In a MAC system, a user has Top Secret clearance but is still denied a specific Top Secret document. Which additional MAC requirement MOST likely explains this?

options.text: Need-to-know — clearance is necessary but not sufficient without a demonstrated need
options.rationale: MAC requires both adequate clearance and need-to-know; lacking need-to-know denies access even at the correct clearance level.

options.text: The user's password was too short
options.rationale: Password length is unrelated to MAC need-to-know enforcement.
MAC does not rely on owner discretion; the factor here is need-to-know.
The scenario is MAC; need-to-know, not an ABAC policy, is the explanation.

stem: An organization needs access decisions that adapt in real time to changing risk signals (device health, geolocation, sensitivity of the resource). Which model is BEST suited?

options.text: ABAC, which evaluates dynamic attributes and context at decision time
options.rationale: ABAC's policy engine can weigh dynamic attributes/context per request, matching adaptive, risk-aware access needs.
Static owner-set ACLs cannot adapt to dynamic risk signals.
MAC's fixed clearance/label model is not designed for dynamic contextual signals.
Removing control does not provide adaptive, risk-aware decisions.

stem: Which model assigns permissions to roles rather than directly to individual users?

options.rationale: RBAC assigns permissions to roles; users receive them through role membership.
DAC assigns access at the owner's discretion per object, not via roles.
MAC uses clearance/label enforcement, not role assignment.
Firewall rule-based control uses global rules, not user roles.

stem: Which factor is LEAST relevant when choosing an access control model for an organization?

options.text: The brand of coffee in the break room
options.rationale: Break-room coffee has no bearing on which access control model fits the organization's needs, making it least relevant.

options.text: The sensitivity of the data and regulatory requirements
options.rationale: Data sensitivity and regulation strongly influence the model choice (e.g., MAC for classified).

options.text: The scale of the organization and administrative burden
options.rationale: Scale affects whether RBAC/ABAC is preferable, a relevant factor.

options.text: The need for dynamic, context-aware decisions
options.rationale: Context needs point toward ABAC, a relevant selection factor.
